processing: Details are sparse; today's Baitang mountain tea includes green tea made from a small-leaved local plant, and as with other greens the leaf is heated to stop oxidation, then shaped and dried.
harvest_season: Not recorded for this tea; spring is the usual prized picking for Guangdong greens.
appearance_dry: Fine, narrow leaf from a small-leaved plant, which local Hakka speakers call fine tea.
appearance_liquor: As with other green teas, a clear pale yellow-green.
taste_profile: Described as strongly fragrant, clean and sweet; little more detail is recorded.

brewing.notes: General advice for fine green tea: water below the boil and an open vessel.

vintage_note: As is usual for green tea, buy the current year's harvest and drink it within the year. Modern tea under this heritage is often sold as Baitang mountain tea, so look for that name and for Boluo on the pack.
description:
Luofu tea takes its name from Luofu Mountain in Boluo county, Huizhou, and it is one of the old names of Guangdong tea. Today the tradition is most clearly tied to Baitang town, whose mountain tea is regarded as its representative.

Baitang tea comes from a low, small-leaved plant with thin, pointed leaves, which Hakka locals call fine tea. Its range around the Xiangtou Mountains also includes a small-leaved purple-bud tea alongside the green.

The cup is described as fragrant, clean and sweet, and little beyond that is recorded. Brew it as you would other delicate greens, with water below the boil.

This is a local tea rather than a market name, and the old name has no strict modern definition. Treat Luofu on a label as a claim about place, and ask where in Boluo the leaf was grown.
history:
Guangdong surveys list Luofu tea among the province's teas produced in the Tang dynasty, together with Lingnan and Xiqiao teas. A local saying has it that Luofu tea began in the Jin, flourished in the Tang and peaked in the Song, when it counted as a famous tea; this rests on local accounts rather than close study.

Modern production centres on Baitang town, which received a Guangdong one-village-one-product recognition in 2009, according to local sources. Acreage figures vary between about 5,000 and 7,000 mu.
